threads.thread_goal: Align on current-state process map and main pain points.

messages.text: Team, I've mapped out our current intake and handover flow from sales floor through to workshop assignment. This covers both phone inquiries and walk-ins. The map is in A1 and reflects what we're doing today—no changes yet. I've identified several bottlenecks where customers wait or information gets lost. Let me know your initial thoughts, especially from the floor.

Thanks for putting this together. I see the flow, but I'm wondering—when a customer calls in, are we capturing all the vehicle details they mention? Sometimes I jot notes on paper and it's hard to pass that cleanly to the workshop. That's probably one of the pain points you mentioned?

From the workshop side, yes—we often get vehicles with incomplete info. Customer says 'it's making a noise' but we don't know if it's on startup, under load, or what. Then we spend 20 minutes just asking questions we should have asked at intake. The map shows this gap clearly. I'd say that's a top pain point for us.

I see three main issues in the map: (1) sellers don't always pass the handover form to us—sometimes it's verbal only; (2) we have no standard triage step, so urgent jobs get mixed with routine ones in the queue; (3) peak times create a jam at the intake desk. Are these the ones you flagged?

The triage gap is real. When I'm the intake tech, I'm doing diagnostics and paperwork at the same time, which slows everything down. If we had a checklist and a clear order of steps, I could move faster and catch missing info before the vehicle goes to a bay.

Exactly those three. Let me refine the map to show where the handoff breaks down and where we lose time. I'll also mark the peak-time congestion points. Once we agree on this current state, we can design the new workflow to fix these gaps. Does everyone agree these are the top three pain points we should prioritize?

Yes, those three cover the main delays we see. If we fix the handover form, add a triage step, and manage the intake queue better, we should see faster throughput. I'm ready to move forward with the design phase.
Agreed. The handover form will help me make sure I'm asking the right questions. I'll need to see what fields are mandatory so I don't miss anything.
Confirmed. These three are the blockers. Once we have a standard form and checklist, we can train everyone and run the pilot. I'll help coordinate the training schedule.
Good. I'll be ready to test the checklist once it's drafted. I can walk through a few recent cases to make sure the steps make sense and don't add extra time.

threads.thread_goal: Define the new intake workflow, handover form, and triage checklist.

messages.text: I've drafted a handover script and form based on what we discussed. The form captures vehicle details, customer contact, and any known issues. The script is short—just a few key questions to ask before handing off to the workshop. See A2 for the full version. I tested it on a couple of calls and it felt natural, not too long.

And here's the intake checklist for technicians. It covers safety checks, basic diagnostics, and documentation. I've laid it out as a step-by-step flow so we don't miss anything. The checklist is in A3. I walked through it with a few recent cases and it took about 8–10 minutes per vehicle, which is reasonable. Feedback welcome.

The handover form looks solid. I see you've got vehicle make/model, mileage, customer description of the issue, and any warranty notes. That covers what we need. One question—do we ask about recent repairs or service history? Sometimes that's relevant for diagnostics.

Good catch. I added a line for 'recent service or repairs' but it's optional. Should I make it mandatory? I don't want the form to get too long, but if it's important for your diagnostics, I can include it.
Yes, make it mandatory. It helps us rule out causes quickly. For example, if they just had brake work, we know to focus elsewhere. It's a small field but saves time.

The checklist looks comprehensive. I see safety gear check, visual inspection, basic electrical test, and documentation steps. One thing—how do we handle urgent jobs? Should the checklist change if it's a warranty claim or a breakdown?

Good question. The checklist is the same for all jobs, but the order might shift. For urgent or warranty cases, we'd flag it at the top and the supervisor assigns it to a priority bay. The checklist itself doesn't change—we still do the safety and basic diagnostics, just faster and with priority routing.

I've reviewed both the form and checklist. They're clear and practical. Before we lock them in, I want to make sure the form fields align with what the checklist expects. Let me cross-check A2 and A3 to ensure no gaps. Also, we need to define the bay allocation rules—that's part of the new workflow. Should we add that to this thread or create a separate one?

I can draft the bay allocation rules. We need to define how we assign vehicles based on job type, urgency, and bay availability. That ties into the workflow diagram. I'll create a simple rule set and share it here so we can review it alongside the form and checklist.

Yes, the rules are important. We need to know: routine jobs go to standard bays, warranty jobs get priority, and breakdowns get the fastest slot. That way, the intake tech can assign the vehicle immediately after the checklist, and we don't have a queue building up.
I'll update the form to include a 'job type' field so the intake tech can quickly categorize it. That way, the assignment is automatic based on the rules.
Perfect. Once I have the bay rules finalized, we can test the whole flow: form → checklist → bay assignment. I'll have the rules ready by EOD tomorrow.

Good. Once we have the updated form, checklist, and bay rules, I'll create the workflow diagram (A1 updated) and we can formally approve all three. That's D3 and D4. Let's aim for approval by end of week so we can move to training and rota planning.
I'm ready to test the updated checklist once the form and rules are finalized. I can run through 5 cases to make sure the flow works end-to-end.
Agreed. Once we approve the form and checklist, I can help with the training content. I'll prepare some example cases so sellers and technicians can practice the new flow.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in lane capacity rules, staff rota, and pilot schedule.

messages.text: I've drafted the staff rota and capacity plan for the pilot. We're running the integrated lane for two weeks starting next Monday. The rota covers peak hours (9am–12pm, 2pm–5pm) and off-peak (12pm–2pm, 5pm–6pm). See A8 for the full schedule. I've assigned sellers, technicians, and supervisors based on current availability. No new hires—we're using existing staff and shifts.

I see the rota. One concern—during peak hours, we have only one intake technician. If we get a rush, that person will be bottlenecked. Can we add a second tech during 9–12 and 2–5? Or do we need to adjust the bay allocation rules to handle overflow?

We can't add headcount, but we can adjust the rules. If intake is full, we route overflow to a holding area or delay the appointment. I've drafted capacity rules in A5 that define how many vehicles we can handle per hour and what happens if we exceed that. Let me share those rules so we can review them together.

The rules make sense. If we're at capacity, we offer a later slot or ask them to call back. That's better than having a long queue in the lane. But we need to communicate this clearly to sellers so they can set customer expectations upfront.
Yes, I can brief customers on wait times when they call or walk in. If we're busy, I'll let them know upfront. That way, they're not surprised and we manage expectations.

Looking at the rota, I'm assigned to intake Monday through Wednesday, then Thursday and Friday. That's good—gives me continuity. But I want to make sure the checklist is finalized before we start. Are we still on track for that?

Yes, the checklist and form should be approved by end of this week. That gives us the weekend to print materials and do a final walkthrough. We'll do a pre-pilot readiness check on Sunday evening to make sure everyone is ready.

I'll coordinate the readiness check. We need to confirm: (1) all materials are printed and in place, (2) everyone has attended the training, (3) the KPI tracker is set up, and (4) we have a daily issue log ready. I'll send a checklist by Friday.
The KPI tracker—is that A4? I want to make sure we're capturing the right metrics. Intake time, rework cases, customer callbacks, and any safety incidents. Those are the key ones for us.

Yes, A4 is the tracker. I've defined those metrics and added a few others: average intake time, vehicles per hour, rework rate, and customer satisfaction score. We'll track daily and review weekly. The supervisor will log data each day.
Who's responsible for collecting customer feedback? I can ask a few questions at the end of the intake, but I want to know what to ask.

That's part of T10. We'll create a short feedback form or script. You'll ask customers about their intake experience—was it clear, did they feel heard, how long did it take? I'll draft that by Friday and share it with you.

Okay, so to confirm: pilot starts Monday, runs for two weeks, rota is locked in A8, capacity rules are in A5, and we do a readiness check Sunday evening. Does everyone agree on the start date and the rota?
Confirmed. I'm ready to start Monday. I'll review the checklist one more time over the weekend.
Confirmed. I'll have the handover form and script ready. Looking forward to testing this.
Yes, I'm ready. The rota works for me. I'll be here to support the intake team and help with any issues that come up.

threads.thread_goal: Monitor pilot progress, surface issues, and adjust quickly.

messages.text: Day 1 of the pilot is complete. Overall, the new intake process worked. We processed 12 vehicles in the morning and 10 in the afternoon. Average intake time was 9 minutes, which is under our 20-minute target. However, I've logged a few issues in the daily log. See A4 for the KPI data and A3 for the checklist feedback.

Day 1 felt good. The checklist worked as designed. One thing I noticed—some customers didn't have all the info on the handover form, so I had to ask follow-up questions. It added a few minutes. Maybe we need a reminder for sellers to fill it out completely?

I see the issue. Some customers don't want to answer all the questions, or they're in a hurry. I'm trying to get the info, but I don't want to hold them up. Maybe we can make some fields optional and focus on the critical ones?

From the workshop side, the critical fields are: vehicle details, customer description of the issue, and recent service history. Everything else is nice-to-have. If we focus on those three, the form will be faster and we'll still get what we need for diagnostics.

Good feedback. Let's adjust the form to mark critical vs. optional fields. That way, sellers know what must be captured and what can be skipped if the customer is in a hurry. I'll update A2 by EOD today.

Another issue from Day 1: we had a peak at 11am with 4 vehicles arriving at once. The intake tech was overwhelmed. We managed, but it was tight. The capacity rules helped—we offered one customer a later slot. They accepted. Should we adjust the rules or add a buffer?

The rules worked as intended. We didn't have a queue, and the customer was okay with the later slot. I'd say we keep the rules as-is for now and monitor the next few days. If we see consistent peaks, we can adjust.
I handled the 11am rush okay. The checklist helped me stay organized. If we get busier, I might need a second tech, but for now, it's manageable.

One more thing—I had a customer ask about warranty coverage during intake. I didn't know the answer, so I had to check with the supervisor. Maybe we need a quick reference guide for sellers on warranty questions?
That's a good point. I'll create a one-page warranty reference for sellers. It won't cover everything, but it'll help with common questions. I'll have it ready by tomorrow.

Overall, Day 1 was a success. We met the intake time target, processed 22 vehicles, and identified a few small tweaks. Let's continue monitoring and adjust as needed. I'll send a daily summary each evening with KPI data and any issues. Next check-in tomorrow evening.
Sounds good. I'll keep an eye on the workshop side and flag any issues with the handover or checklist. If I see patterns, I'll let you know.
Will do. I'll note any checklist issues or timing problems and report back tomorrow.
Thanks for the summary. I'll focus on getting the form filled out completely and managing customer expectations on wait times.

Day 3 update: We've processed 58 vehicles over three days. Average intake time is holding at 9 minutes. The form adjustment (critical vs. optional fields) is working—sellers are faster and customers are happier. No major issues. One small thing: the checklist could use a note on electrical safety for certain vehicle types. I'll flag that for review with the technician.

Yes, I noticed that too. Some vehicles have complex electrical systems and I want to make sure I'm checking the right things. I can add a note to the checklist for high-voltage systems. I'll update it by EOD.

Good progress. The pilot is on track. Let's continue with daily monitoring and make small adjustments as needed. By the end of week one, we should have enough data to assess whether the process is working. Any major issues or safety concerns, flag them immediately.

From the workshop side, everything is running smoothly. The handover form is clear, the checklist is thorough, and we're getting vehicles assigned to the right bays quickly. No safety issues so far. I'll continue to monitor and report any concerns.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results, customer feedback, and next steps.

messages.text: The two-week pilot is complete. I've compiled the final report with KPI data, customer feedback, and recommendations. See A4 for the metrics and A7 for the customer feedback summary. Overall, the integrated lane process is working well. Intake time averaged 8.5 minutes, well under the 20-minute target. Rework cases dropped by 15% compared to the previous month. Customer satisfaction scores are positive. Let me walk through the key findings.

Great results. From the workshop perspective, the handover quality improved significantly. We're getting complete information upfront, which means fewer diagnostic delays. The triage checklist is helping us assign vehicles to the right bays faster. I'd say the process is ready to roll out.

The checklist worked well. I felt organized and efficient. The only adjustment we made was adding the electrical safety note, which helped with complex vehicles. I'm confident in the process. Ready to make it permanent.

The form worked well once we marked critical vs. optional fields. Customers appreciated the clarity, and I was able to move faster. The feedback I collected shows customers liked the streamlined intake. A few mentioned they appreciated knowing the wait time upfront.

The rota and capacity rules held up well. We managed peak times without bottlenecks. The daily issue log shows only minor adjustments needed. I'd recommend we keep the current staffing model and rules for the permanent rollout.

Excellent feedback. Based on the pilot results and your input, I recommend we roll out the integrated lane process permanently. The KPIs are strong, customer feedback is positive, and the team is confident. We should also assign a process owner to maintain and update the documentation. I'm proposing that I take on that role, with monthly reviews to keep everything current.

I agree. The process is solid and the team is aligned. Rolling out permanently makes sense. Having a process owner to maintain the documentation is important—we don't want things to drift after the pilot.
Agreed. The process is working. I'm ready to continue with the new intake checklist permanently. Monthly reviews sound good—we can catch any issues early.
Yes, let's roll it out. The form is working well and customers are happy. I'm confident in the handover process now.
Confirmed. The rota and capacity rules are solid. I'll support the permanent rollout and help with any training updates. Monthly reviews will keep us on track.

Great. So we're moving forward with permanent rollout. Here's the action plan: (1) Update all documentation with the final versions of the form, checklist, and rules. (2) Schedule a full-team briefing for next week to confirm the permanent process. (3) I'll set up monthly review meetings starting in two weeks. (4) We'll monitor KPIs for the next month to ensure consistency. Any questions or concerns?
Sounds good. I'll help with the full-team briefing and make sure the workshop team understands the permanent process. No concerns from my side.
I'm ready. I'll continue with the checklist and support the briefing. Looking forward to the monthly reviews.
All set. I'll be at the briefing and ready to support the permanent process. Thanks for leading this project.
No concerns. I'll coordinate the briefing and help with any training updates. The team is ready.

Perfect. I'll send out the final report and action plan by EOD today. Full-team briefing is scheduled for next Tuesday at 10am. See you all there. Great work on the pilot—this is a solid improvement for our customers and our team.
